content: A mirror is an object with a surface that exhibits excellent specular reflection, meaning it is smooth enough to form a clear image. The most common type of mirror is the plane mirror, which has a flat surface. Curved mirrors, such as concave or convex mirrors, are also used to magnify or reduce images, focus light, or distort the reflected image. Mirrors are widely utilized for personal grooming, decoration, and architectural purposes. They are also integral components in scientific instruments like telescopes, lasers, cameras, and industrial machinery. While most mirrors are designed for visible light, specialized mirrors are created for other wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation, particularly in optical instruments. The earliest mirrors were made from polished stones like obsidian, a naturally occurring volcanic glass. Obsidian mirrors dating back to around 6000 BC have been discovered in Anatolia (modern-day Turkey). Polished stone mirrors from Central and South America date to approximately 2000 BC. Polished copper mirrors were crafted in Mesopotamia around 4000 BC and in ancient Egypt around 3000 BC. In China, bronze mirrors were produced starting around 2000 BC. Metal-coated glass mirrors are believed to have been invented in Sidon (modern-day Lebanon) in the first century AD. Roman author Pliny mentioned glass mirrors backed with gold leaf in his work Natural History around 77 AD. During the early Renaissance, European manufacturers perfected a method of coating glass with a tin-mercury amalgam, with Venice becoming a center for mirror production in the 16th century. These mirrors were considered luxury items. In 1835, German chemist Justus von Liebig developed the silvered-glass mirror by depositing a thin layer of metallic silver onto glass through the chemical reduction of silver nitrate. This innovation allowed for mass production and made mirrors more affordable. Modern mirrors are often produced by vacuum deposition of aluminum or silver onto a glass substrate. Most mirrors are manufactured by applying a reflective coating to a suitable substrate, typically glass, due to its rigidity, ease of fabrication, and ability to achieve a smooth finish. The reflective coating is usually applied to the back surface of the glass to protect it from corrosion and damage. The substrate is shaped, polished, and cleaned before being coated. Glass mirrors are commonly coated with silver or aluminum, using a series of layers: tin, silver, a chemical activator, copper, and paint. Tin is applied to ensure the silver adheres to the glass, while the activator hardens the tin/silver layer. Copper adds durability, and paint protects the coating from scratches and damage. In cost-sensitive or highly durable applications, mirrors may be made from polished metal. For technical applications like laser mirrors, the reflective coating is applied to the front surface of the substrate to eliminate double reflections and reduce light absorption. Protective overcoats may be added to prevent oxidation of the reflective layer. In a plane mirror, a parallel beam of light changes direction while remaining parallel, forming virtual images of the same size as the original object. Concave mirrors focus parallel light beams to a single point, while convex mirrors cause parallel beams to diverge. Spherical concave and convex mirrors suffer from spherical aberration, preventing perfect focus, but parabolic reflectors can focus parallel rays to a nearly ideal point. Parabolic reflectors are unsuitable for imaging nearby objects due to the non-parallel nature of light rays. Light reflects off a mirror at an angle equal to its angle of incidence, a principle derived from the interference of a plane wave on a flat boundary. Mirrors have numerous applications. Rear-view mirrors in vehicles allow drivers to see behind them, while convex mirrors provide a wider field of view and are used at road junctions, parking lots, and in security systems. Dentists use mouth mirrors for indirect vision and lighting inside the mouth, and engineers use them to inspect tight spaces. Two-way mirrors, also known as one-way mirrors, reflect some light while allowing the rest to pass through. They are used between a brightly lit room and a dark room, enabling observation from the dark side while appearing as a regular mirror on the bright side. These mirrors are also used in optical instruments as beam splitters for applications like interferometry. Mirrors are used for signaling by reflecting sunlight, a technique employed historically by Native American tribes and militaries. They are also included in survival kits for rescue purposes. In technology, microscopic mirrors are key components in high-definition televisions and video projectors, such as those using Texas Instruments' DLP technology. Telescopes and precision instruments use front-silvered mirrors to eliminate reflections from the glass surface. These mirrors are often coated with aluminum or silver and require special handling due to their fragility. Protective overcoats are applied to prevent corrosion, and the reflectivity of the coating can be tailored for specific wavelengths. In art, mirrors have played a significant role. Filippo Brunelleschi used mirrors to discover linear perspective, and Leonardo da Vinci referred to the mirror as the master of painters. Mirrors are central to iconic European paintings like Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait and Diego Velázquez's Las Meninas. They have also been used in self-portraits by artists like Rembrandt and Frida Kahlo. Contemporary artists use mirrors in sculptures, installations, and paintings. Mirrors are also used in entertainment, such as in amusement park attractions like halls of mirrors and mirror mazes, as well as in magic tricks like Pepper's ghost. Superstitions surrounding mirrors include the belief that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck, possibly due to the idea that mirrors reflect part of the soul. Vampires are said to lack reflections because they are soulless. Experiments have shown that only certain animals, such as elephants, dolphins, and chimpanzees, can recognize themselves in mirrors. Unusual types of mirrors include acoustic mirrors for sound reflection, active mirrors that amplify light, and atomic mirrors for reflecting matter waves. Cold mirrors reflect visible light while transmitting infrared, and hot mirrors do the opposite. Corner reflectors use three flat mirrors to reflect light back to its source, and X-ray mirrors reflect X-rays at grazing angles.
